findings.evidence: "The benefits team tracks the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year." / "The finance liaison reviews the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year." / "The people operations office tracks the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year."
findings.fix: Pick one owner for stipend-budget tracking, state it once, and delete the two duplicate/contradictory restatements.
findings.location: Program Overview, paragraph 1 ("The benefits team tracks the stipend budget...") compared with the "Special Cases" section ("The finance liaison reviews the stipend budget...") and "Questions and Updates" section ("The people operations office tracks the stipend budget...")
findings.violation: The same near-identical sentence is repeated three times across the document, each time naming a different owner (benefits team, finance liaison, people operations office) for what is described as the same task.

findings.evidence: "The stipend clock resumes on their first day back."
findings.fix: Define "stipend clock" explicitly or replace the phrase with a concrete reference to the specific eligibility timer it means.
findings.location: Eligibility section, third paragraph, final sentence
findings.violation: "Stipend clock" is never defined anywhere in the document, so it's unclear whether this refers to the 90-day service requirement, the benefit-year cycle, or something else.

findings.evidence: "In addition, eligibility for the workspace stipend depends on several details..."
findings.fix: Use one consistent stipend name throughout, or explicitly explain the relationship between the "workspace stipend" and the "home-office equipment stipend."
findings.location: Eligibility section, fourth paragraph, opening sentence
findings.violation: The document's title and every other section refer to the "home-office equipment stipend," but this paragraph suddenly introduces a "workspace stipend" without clarifying whether it's the same benefit or a separate one.

findings.evidence: Nine consecutive sentences beginning "The workspace must...", "A workspace located...", "A workspace used only occasionally...", etc., all run together in one paragraph
findings.fix: Break the rules into a numbered or bulleted list, one rule per item.
findings.location: Eligibility section, fourth paragraph (the workspace-review list)
findings.violation: A long sequence of distinct, independent eligibility rules is packed into a single dense paragraph, making it hard to audit or reference any one rule.

findings.evidence: "A workspace confirmation from more than one year ago no longer satisfies the stipend requirement on its own."
findings.fix: Either state what additional step revalidates an old confirmation, or drop "on its own" and state plainly that confirmations expire after one year.
findings.location: Eligibility section, fourth paragraph, last sentence
findings.violation: "On its own" implies some additional factor could make an old confirmation acceptable, but no such factor is ever described.

findings.evidence: "Employees must submit the receipt, the manager's approval form, and the original purchase order before the review begins." vs. "The manager reviews the request within two business days."
findings.fix: Lay out the process as an ordered sequence (e.g., request submitted → manager reviews and approves → employee purchases → receipt/PO submitted) so approval and review aren't described as both preceding and following each other.
findings.location: How to Apply section, paragraph 1, compared with Approval Timeline section, paragraph 1
findings.violation: The application step already requires the manager's signed approval form before "the review" starts, yet the Approval Timeline describes the manager reviewing the request afterward - it's unclear whether approval happens once or twice, and in what order relative to the purchase itself.

findings.evidence: "Then, the employee reviews the confirmation summary before submitting the final request."
findings.fix: Clarify how many distinct submission steps exist (initial documents vs. final request) and put them in a single consistent order.
findings.violation: This implies the receipt/approval-form/PO submission described in paragraph 1 happens before a later "final request," contradicting paragraph 1's framing that those documents are submitted "before the review begins."

findings.evidence: "The manager reviews the request within two business days." followed by "The requester gets an automatic reminder after three days."
findings.fix: Use consistent units (e.g., both in business days) and state explicitly how the reminder timing relates to the two-day review window.
findings.violation: The timeline mixes "business days" and plain "days" for closely related deadlines, leaving it unclear whether the reminder fires before, at, or after the manager's review deadline.

findings.evidence: "A photo of the receipt is enough for most requests." vs. "Employees must submit the receipt, the manager's approval form, and the original purchase order before the review begins."
findings.fix: State one consistent documentation requirement (original vs. photo) and reconcile it across both sections.
findings.location: Required Documentation section, compared with How to Apply section
findings.violation: One section says a photo of the receipt suffices, while another requires "the original purchase order" and "the receipt," implying originals are needed - these conflict on what documentation form is actually acceptable.

findings.evidence: "Additionally, employees shall retain receipts for one year after the purchase date."
findings.fix: Match the sentence's tone to the rest of the document and clarify whether one year is the total retention period or an addition to indefinite retention.
findings.violation: This sentence uses legalistic "shall" phrasing inconsistent with the rest of the document's tone, and it's unclear how a one-year retention rule relates to the preceding, undated instruction to "keep proof of purchase for every stipend item."

findings.evidence: "Similarly, the policy applies to one device per category per employee whenever the benefits team confirms that the role genuinely requires a second device..."
findings.fix: Rewrite as two clear rules: the default one-device-per-category limit, and a separately stated exception process for a second device, reconciled with the one-claim-per-year eligibility rule.
findings.location: Restrictions and Exceptions section, second paragraph
findings.violation: The sentence states the policy limits employees to "one device per category" while simultaneously describing conditions under which a "second device" is allowed in the same category - a direct internal contradiction. It also conflicts with Eligibility's earlier statement that "the stipend covers one claim per employee per benefit year."

findings.evidence: "Similarly, the policy applies to one device per category..." (following the sentence about annual photo checks of equipment condition)
findings.fix: Replace "Similarly" with a transition that doesn't falsely imply parallelism, or move the sentence to its own section.
findings.location: Restrictions and Exceptions section, second paragraph, opening word
findings.violation: "Similarly" implies this sentence parallels the prior one about equipment condition checks, but it actually introduces an unrelated topic (device quantity limits), making the transition illogical.

findings.evidence: "You record the stipend item on the request form... Also, you submit the request in the portal. You track its status there until the payment clears."
findings.fix: Rewrite the section in third person to match the rest of the document.
findings.violation: This section switches to second-person "you," while every other section uses third-person "employees" or "the employee," creating an inconsistent voice.

findings.evidence: "You record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log each month."
findings.fix: Either define "stipend item" on first use or replace it with one of the document's existing terms.
findings.violation: "Stipend item" is a new term not defined or used elsewhere in the document (which otherwise says "equipment," "device," or "receipt"), leaving its meaning ambiguous.

findings.evidence: "Completing the request begins with confirming eligibility, and uploading the receipt."
findings.fix: Merge this section with "How to Apply" into one authoritative, consistently ordered process, and remove the unnecessary comma.
findings.violation: This two-step process contradicts the multi-step, differently ordered process described in "How to Apply" (which never mentions "confirming eligibility" as an applicant action), and the comma before "and" incorrectly punctuates a two-item list.

findings.evidence: "Once approved, the team schedules the reimbursement for the next pay cycle." vs. "The finance office conducts an evaluation of every submitted receipt before it approves the amount." vs. "Payroll releases the stipend item amount after that monthly review."
findings.fix: Define a single, explicit payment workflow naming which party evaluates, approves, and disburses funds, and in what sequence.
findings.location: Program Coordination section, last sentence, compared with Reimbursement Amounts and Terminology Notes sections
findings.violation: Three different sections assign payment-related responsibility to three different actors (benefits team, finance office, payroll) without clarifying how these roles relate or hand off to one another.

findings.evidence: "The escalation of repeat requests happens automatically within the same quarter."
findings.fix: Define "repeat request" and describe what the escalation entails and who handles it.
findings.violation: "Repeat requests" is never defined or referenced anywhere else in the document, so it's unclear what qualifies as a repeat request or why/how it gets escalated.

findings.evidence: "The determination of stipend eligibility happens before any payment goes out. The escalation of repeat requests happens automatically within the same quarter."
findings.fix: Rewrite both sentences in active voice naming who performs the determination and who/what triggers the escalation.
findings.violation: Both sentences use vague passive/nominalized phrasing with no named actor, inconsistent with the rest of the document's pattern of naming a specific responsible party (manager, finance office, benefits team, etc.).

findings.evidence: "The people operations office tracks the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year. Every entry carries a date stamp so the record stays easy to audit."
findings.fix: Replace this section's content with actual guidance on questions/updates (e.g., contact point, update log location), and remove the duplicated budget sentence.
findings.violation: A section titled "Questions and Updates" contains no information about how to ask questions or how policy updates are communicated; instead it repeats, near-verbatim, the budget/catalog sentences from "Program Overview," and "Every entry carries a date stamp" now dangles without a clear referent (Program Overview attached it to catalog entries, not budget tracking).
